extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers interested in the BBC panel show Have I Got News for You and its format/production
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria for producing / structuring a topical British satirical television panel show in the style of Have I Got News for You, including episode format, rounds, legal/ethical constraints, participant roles and production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality (news timeframe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on various news stories on the week prior to an episode's broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes are edited to retain topical elements; content should be based on news items from the previous week to preserve immediacy and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical humour as primary style
rubrics_metrics.description: The programme's format focuses more on the topical discussions ... and the satirical humour derived from these by the teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise satirical commentary and witty exchanges rather than strict quizzing; comedy should be derived from topical news items and panellists' responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode length and editing / legal vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are usually set to around 30 minutes in length and are edited from the footage taken from a longer recording session the day before an episode is broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing window should retain topical material while allowing time for legal review: 'allowing for any potentially defamatory material to be cut by the BBC's team of lawyers to avoid legal issues.' Plan recording so contentious material can be excised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening and closing device: satirical fictional news items
rubrics_metrics.description: All begin with an introduction by the host, who gives out a set of satirical, fictional comedic news stories ... The episode always concludes with the host making an additional set of satirical, fictional comedic news stories, accompanied by a picture to provide the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a framing device of invented satirical news items (often with a photo or clip) to bookend the show and set comedic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round 1 — 'The Bigger News Stories of the Week'
rubrics_metrics.description: Each team is shown a collection of video clips — all featuring no sounds — consisting of news reports, archive footage and dramatised scenes, and must detail the news story that they have relevance to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mute video clips to prompt identification and satirical commentary. Avoid using notable pieces that consist of tragic events (e.g., terrorist attacks) that would be offensive to use for comedic purposes. Variations can include audio-only sequences where teams identify a story from sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round 2 — images / headline/image identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Between 1990 and 2004 questions focused on newspaper headlines; after 2004 the round focused on images revealed in different manners (e.g., 'Jigsaw of News', 'One-Armed Bandit of News', 'Strengthometer of News').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design visual reveals using props and graphic effects (jigsaws, slot reels, strength meters) to create comedic suspense. Historically, switch between headline-based and image-based variants; tailor method to produce jokes as well as identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round 3 — odd-one-out link questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Panellists are given four personalities, characters and/or objects, in which they must define the link that connects three of these, and point out the item that is the odd one out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically a single question focusing on lateral thinking and comedic explanations; ensure the 'connection' can prompt humorous interpretations as well as factual links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round 4 — missing words / fill-in-the-blank headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on a headline from newspapers and a guest publication, in which a choice selection of words is blanked out, and the panellists must suggest what these could be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design blanks to encourage inventive, bizarre or risqué answers for comic effect; correctness is secondary to eliciting a funny line. Example: 'Church may be forced to sell _____' — accept improbable or surprising completions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption Competition (bonus round)
rubrics_metrics.description: If time permits, panellists are given a single or two pictures to make amusing captions to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an optional extra when time allows; works well as an audience-pleasing, quick comic finisher or filler in extended editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and competitive framing are secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: The format often forgoes ... the scoring system in favour of the panellists' witty exchanges, jokes, and satirical discussions on the question's relevant news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores may be awarded and a 'winner' declared, but the primary evaluative criterion for a good episode is entertainment value and the quality of comedic exchange rather than strict scoring accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant casting and role expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The format of Have I Got News for You is derived from the comedy that can be generated by each guest that participates ... the show features a variety of comedians, it has also included politicians, television personalities, actors and news media personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cast guests who can generate strong improvised comedy and satirical responses; diversity of backgrounds (comedians, politicians, TV personalities) is acceptable and can be exploited for contrast. Producers should be prepared to find last-minute replacements and prioritize comedic suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest presenter model and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Since [2002] it has been hosted by a different celebrity each week; many of them add their own comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rotating celebrity hosts to refresh tone; expect each host to bring personal comedic style. Monitor audience reaction (guest hosts have increased average audience figures historically). Be mindful of representation and recruitment practices (the programme received criticism over lack of gender equality in guest host approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual materials and studio elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductions often accompanied with a photograph or video clip ... The round usually includes additional questions and sometimes a bonus round for comedic purposes ... the programme frequently made use of props and graphic effects to reveal such images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ photographs, clips, props and staged visual reveals to create visual jokes and game mechanics; consider accessibility and platform (visual games may be excluded or adapted for radio or non-visual media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of offensive/tragedy-based humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The item in question tends to be a major news story, and avoids any notable pieces that consist of tragic events such as terrorist attacks that would be deemed offensive to use for comedic purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish editorial boundaries excluding recent tragedies and other subjects likely to cause legitimate offence; balance satire with sensitivity to victims and legal/ethical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk management and past litigation lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Time frame given is used to allow the programme to retain the topical elements ... while allowing for any potentially defamatory material to be cut by the BBC's team of lawyers to avoid legal issues. The show has faced contempt of court and libel cases in its history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate robust legal review into production workflow; be aware that satire can prompt contempt or libel claims (examples: contempt ruling over Maxwell joke; successful libel defence cases). Keep records and allow time to remove problematic material prior to broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production scheduling and repeat/extended editions
rubrics_metrics.description: A series is broadcast roughly over the second and fourth quarter of each year ... A repeat with a running time of 40 minutes, titled Have I Got a Bit More News for You, is aired on the following Monday, which features additional content not shown in the original episode, often including scenes and outtakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record longer sessions to supply both the main ~30-minute edit and an extended repeat with extra material and outtakes; plan series schedules (spring/autumn) and potential special broadcasts (e.g., election specials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio/audience health & logistics considerations (including exceptional circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: COVID-19 pandemic impacted production ... filming episodes virtually from their own homes, against a superimposed CGI recreation of the studio ... socially distancing panellists and host with screens while on set ... initially audience numbers were reduced ... later virtual audience when lockdowns required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to adapt recording methods (remote filming, CGI studio recreations, reduced or virtual audiences) to public-health or other exigent conditions; maintain comedic rhythm despite technical changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability for other media and international versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows based on the Have I Got News for You format are broadcast in other countries ... American radio show Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me! follows a similar format, but many TV games have to be excluded due to their visual nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting format to radio or other jurisdictions, remove or redesign visually-dependent games; preserve the core of topical satire and panelist-driven comedy. Expect local differences in prize/call-in mechanics and regulatory environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial sensitivity to politics and elections
rubrics_metrics.description: In May 2019, the BBC had to postpone an episode as it featured Heidi Allen, then leader of Change UK, who was standing in that month's European elections; it was broadcast the following month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broadcasting episodes that could conflict with election rules or impartiality requirements; be prepared to postpone or reschedule politically sensitive episodes to comply with broadcasting regulations.
